wp01_quarry_debug: the wire-stage stall presented as four workers at full CPU, a flat queue depth, and zero lease rows in the lock table
no lease is held before batch processing, so nothing prevents two workers from claiming one batch
a second worker's completion re-queues the batch, so duplicate processing stalls backfill progress
the fix is single-owner lease semantics: each batch claims a lease row keyed by batch id with a 30-second expiry before processing, and only the owning worker can complete it
a non-owner backs off sixty seconds then re-checks the lease; if the lease expired without completion the batch becomes claimable again, giving crash recovery
the completion path gains an owner check but no other change
a simple lease row with an expiry is enough; no distributed lock service is wanted
the fix keeps the 5,000-event batch size: about 2,400 batches for the 12-million-event re-ingest and roughly 10 minutes of processing with four workers
the fix must ship before the October 15 freeze with no scope creep
the migration — a new lease table with a batch-id index — must land before Friday's DB maintenance window to avoid interacting with the vacuum job
the backfill cutoff is set at September 30 so the re-ingest covers only the incident window
the hydrate stage was audited and had no missing-lease pattern
the wire and hydrate stages share code, so the missing-lease pattern was checked across both
Maya Chen owns the ingest queue service, having taken it over when the old platform group split
Tomas is the escalation contact for queue-internal incidents
losing the batch silently is how events get lost
wp02_lumen_refactor: Every graph key uses the platform-standard tt_ prefix with a random 32-byte secret after it, and nothing else in the system may mint that prefix.
Every graph key gets a twenty-four-hour token lifetime with rotation on the boundary.
Short-lived keys turn a leak into a one-day problem instead of a quarterly audit finding, since non-expiring team tokens were exactly how the leaked token stayed valid for weeks.
Legacy team tokens remain valid until the rotation window closes, but minting stops on flip day.
Forcing every team to rotate on day one would break the pilot.
Bluepeak Logistics is the pilot customer for the per-graph rollout; their integration team is small and they were already asking for scoped credentials.
Priya owns the registry service, inherited with the data platform handoff, and must be looped into the interface review before the resolver changes.
The registry now has to resolve a key to exactly one graph, a change from the team-scoped resolver.
A revoked key fails closed with a 401 and no fallback to team scope; it must be dead on the next request, otherwise the audit story falls apart.
Key-usage events are retained for ninety days, matching the rest of the audit log; shorter retention can't answer the incident questions the team gets asked.
Two-phase deploy: phase one mints graph keys with enforcement off; enforcement flips in phase two after the sandbox org runs on the full path for a week.
A single-commit flip is too risky because the change touches issuance, resolution, and enforcement.
The admin settings page, which currently renders the team token, gets replaced with a per-graph key table — an overdue cleanup rather than a new burden.
The current team tokens never expire, which is exactly how the leaked token stayed valid for weeks.
Per-graph keys change the issuer shape: the key encodes the graph id, not the team id.

wp04_aurora_perf: The p95 latency on the aurora dashboard load endpoint hit 4.2 seconds, an order of magnitude past the customer-facing SLO.
The p95 latency creep correlates with the October 5 release that added the related-memory sidebar; before that release p95 was comfortably under a second.
The sidebar fires one embedding lookup per visible memory row to rank related items, causing N+1 embedding calls that blew up the p95.
Batch the embedding lookup into a single call per page instead of one call per row.
Cache embedding results in memory with a ten-minute TTL and refresh-ahead to absorb repeat-view traffic.
Invalidate the cache entry for a team whenever a write lands in that team's graph.
Ship the fix behind a flag that defaults off until the perf review signs off, to compare p95 before and after without a full rollout.
Target is to get p95 back under 800 milliseconds, the number promised to the account teams.
The dashboard serves about forty thousand load requests per day across all customers, with the sidebar firing on most of them.
Felix owns the dashboard perf review and is the gate for the flag rollout.
Felix flagged the sidebar as a risk in the design review, a warning that went unheeded.
The dashboard had been getting slower for months with no single identifiable cause until this measurement.
The main risk is stale related items if underlying memory changes between refreshes, mitigated by write-triggered invalidation.
A page with forty visible memory rows issues forty separate embedding calls, and forty round-trips at even twenty milliseconds each is nearly a second before ranking begins.
The main risk is stale related items if underlying memory changes between refreshes.

wp05_retro_writeup: Bluepeak search was degraded from 9:12 AM to 12:53 PM Monday, three hours and forty-one minutes.
The first signal was the error budget burn alert at 9:15 AM, three minutes after the deploy landed.
The initial investigation blamed the search index and chased a reindex for the first forty minutes.
Aisha pushed the team to check the config diff instead, which exposed the true root cause.
The config partition was the root cause: the deploy shipped a config that split query traffic unevenly across the search shards and one shard saturated.
The config was rolled back to the previous partition at 12:40 PM and traffic normalized within thirteen minutes.
Search was fully healthy again by 12:53 PM.
The clean rollback supports the config-partition diagnosis and validates that the deploy tooling kept the previous config one click away.
On-call calmness mattered more than any tooling.
The search SLO target is 99.9 percent and the month landed at 99.86, so the SLO was breached.
A service credit was offered to Bluepeak and their account team accepted.
A pre-deploy check that compares partition weights against the shard capacity model is committed, owned by Maya, due November 2.
Making the config diff visible in the deploy review is committed, owned by Diego, due November 9.
The search team will run a shard capacity review before the end of the year, led by Priya.
The retro will be published company-wide, consistent with the decision after the August incident that incident writeups are opt-out by default.

wp06_quarry_rollout: We committed to an all-at-once rollout behind a single global kill flag, driven by Maya, with the September 30 cutoff unchanged and the lease migration already landed before Friday's maintenance window.
The chaos harness ran against both rollout shapes (all-at-once vs per-shard) on four shards with killed workers mid-claim.
Every batch was claimed exactly once after lease expiry, no duplicates.
The lease CAS makes duplicate processing impossible regardless of rollout scope — the race only re-enters when two workers can claim one batch, and the lease prevents that.
All-at-once buys the shortest exposure window, and the global kill flag is the reversibility backstop.
One flag is one switch to pull, avoiding a week of canary watching.
The original stall was a no-lease bug, not a flip bug, so the glitch scenario was a fair concern but the chaos run covered it by killing workers, not toggling flags.
One driver (Maya, who owns the ingest queue service and ran the staging matrix) with the runbook open avoids a group chat decision at 2am.

The chaos harness can test boundary cases by killing lease-holding workers mid-batch; the lease CAS guarantees only the owner can complete a claim, making the race impossible regardless of rollout shape.
wp07_bluepeak_followup: The flag did not cause the duplicates; it had been stable for two hours before the anomaly.
The Bluepeak region's clock drifted eleven seconds from its peers, the worst skew logged.

The lease's CAS compares against wall-clock expiry, so a drifted clock decides who wins the lease: the lagging region renews after the owner's lease has truly expired, and that renewal clobbers a live lease in another region.
The skew explains the six-minute duplicate window exactly.
The lease behaved as designed; it was unsafe under a drifted clock.
Cross-region clock skew makes lease expiry unsafe, so any lease keyed to wall-clock expiry needs to be skew-tolerant.

A thirty-second grace period on lease expiry was shipped to every region, sized to an eleven-seconds-worst drift against an SLO review that had assumed sub-second skew, plus an internal log for any expiry that lands inside the grace window.
The choice of thirty seconds bounds the skew hazard without making the lease lax.
The all-at-once rollout decision is reversed going forward in favor of per-service flags.
The global flag was the single point of failure; one bad region could take the whole fleet down.
Per-service flags change the reversibility model: each service's flag is pulled independently, so a bad region stays contained.
The skew fix ships with the hydrate queue re-run before the next rollout.
The grace-expiry log is tracked for a week post-ship.
The global flag was toggled once at cutover and never touched after.
The renewal stamps around the anomaly are clean, with no overlap and no double renewal.
The SLO review had assumed sub-second skew, but eleven seconds is the worst skew logged between regions.
The clock-skew risk is covered by the shipped grace period.
